title: I used to put my stop loss right below the obvious level. After getting hunted again and again, I finally changed it.
author: Electronic_Tea_2948
selftext:
This one cost me a lot before I figured it out. I would go long near 24,200, put my stop just under the nearby low at 24,150, and then watch price dip to 24,145, take me out, and shoot straight back up without me. Every single time it felt personal.

Then it clicked. My stop was sitting exactly where everyone else put theirs.

Think about it. If the obvious low is at 24,150, then thousands of us are putting our stops right under it in the same tiny zone. That creates a big pile of stops in one spot, and price often gets pushed down just enough to trigger all of them before reversing. I was basically handing the market an easy target.

So I changed two things. I either give my stop more room below the noise, or I take a smaller position so I can place that wider stop without risking more money. The point is to not sit in the exact pocket where everyone is clustered.

I tried this and my random stop outs dropped a lot. The trades I was right about finally had the room to work. Does anyone else think about where the crowd puts their stops, or do you still use the textbook level?

comments.author: AssMan2025
comments.body: Good thinking but what’s the chance everyone purchased at the same price

comments.author: BetInformal6081
comments.body: this is an interesting lesson in risk management giving trades enough room to handle normal volatility makes sense provided position sizing adjusts accordingly..

comments.author: BleaklyAdhesive
comments.body: I think the important part is adjusting position size when you give the stop more room. Simply moving it further away without reducing exposure can make the losses much worse. The maximum loss price on Moon makes me think about how close a leveraged position is to being closed. Whether it's a stop loss or a wager limit, the invalidation level should come from the setup rather than frustration with previous trades.
